title: Reason, for Shia jurists
hookLine: Ja'fari jurists count reason as a source alongside the Qur'an, sunnah and consensus

lines: WILL YOU NOT USE YOUR REASON?
cards: Open al-Kafi, a collection of reports gathered by the scholar al-Kulayni and read closely by Shia Muslims, and the very first section is not about prayer, or fasting, or law. It's called the book of reason and ignorance.
Before a single ruling, the collection stops to talk about the mind. The Qur'an itself asks its listeners, in Surah al-Baqarah, whether they have no sense, whether they will not use their reason.
For Ja'fari jurists, the Shia school of law named for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, that question isn't only a rebuke. It's a door into the law. Today's word is reason.

teach.b: The Arabic word is 'aql, the mind, the faculty that understands.
Ja'fari legal theory names its sources: the Qur'an, the sunnah, consensus, and 'aql, reason. Sunni schools reason too, of course, mostly through analogy, which was yesterday.
The Ja'fari path sets analogy aside and gives reason its own seat at the table. What does reason do there? Not invent rulings out of thin air.
Ja'fari jurists use it in a few careful ways.

teach.h: WHAT A DUTY CAN'T BE DONE WITHOUT.
teach.b: One sounds almost too plain to need saying: when the law requires something, it requires whatever that thing can't be done without.
Pilgrimage is a duty for those who are able, so the journey to Mecca becomes part of the duty, though no verse says book the ticket and pack the bag. Reason sees the link, and the jurist follows it.
Another is the judgment that some things are good or bad in themselves: justice is good, injustice is wrong, and a mind can see this.

Ja'fari theology holds that God does not command injustice, and that reason can recognize justice. From there comes a principle stated as a pair: what reason firmly judges, the law also judges, and the reverse.
Jurists argue hard over what counts as a firm judgment of reason, and don't let a passing opinion count as one. So here is the fair picture. Sunni and Ja'fari jurists both use the mind.
They differ in where they place it: inside analogy, for the Sunni schools that use it, or beside the texts as a source with its own name.
Both are trying to read the same revelation without leaving their minds at the door.

how: Ja'fari jurists list the Qur'an, the sunnah, consensus and reason as the sources of law, and Shia Muslims follow the rulings of living jurists trained in this method.

games.why: when the law requires something, it requires what that thing can't be done without. reason sees the link.

practice: Pick something you've committed to, being on time for someone or keeping a promise to call, and ask what it can't be done without: leaving earlier, charging the phone, writing it down.
Notice that you never chose those links on their own; the first commitment chose them for you. If you pray, you might ask for a clear mind.
